# Temperature and Magnetic Field Dependence of Coulomb Drag Near Half-Filling of the Lowest Landau Level

## Overview of the Theoretical Framework

The authors present a comprehensive theoretical investigation into the behavior of Coulomb drag transresistivity in double-layer two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) systems operating within the quantum Hall regime, with particular focus on the physics occurring near half filling of the lowest Landau level. This regime is of significant interest because it corresponds to a composite fermion liquid state, where the strongly correlated electron system can be effectively described in terms of composite fermions—electrons bound to an even number of magnetic flux quanta. The study systematically examines how both temperature and applied magnetic field influence the transresistivity, which serves as the primary experimental signature of interlayer momentum transfer mediated by Coulomb interactions between the two spatially separated electron layers.

## Role of Fermi-Liquid Interactions

A central finding of this work concerns the critical role played by Fermi-liquid interactions between the relevant quasiparticles in shaping the observed transresistivity behavior. Near half filling, the appropriate quasiparticles are composite fermions, which themselves interact through residual gauge-field-mediated and Coulomb interactions beyond the mean-field composite fermion picture. The authors demonstrate that these interaction effects are not merely perturbative corrections but instead substantially modify the predicted dependence of the transresistivity on the relevant system parameters. This finding underscores the importance of treating the composite fermion system as an interacting Fermi liquid, rather than relying solely on a non-interacting or weakly-interacting composite fermion model, in order to accurately capture the drag phenomenology in this regime.

## Independence from Interlayer Spacing

One of the most notable and experimentally relevant results emerging from this theoretical analysis is the demonstration that Fermi-liquid interactions drive the transresistivity toward a regime of insensitivity to the interlayer separation distance. Specifically, the authors show that across the range of interlayer spacings typically employed in experimental double-layer heterostructures, the transresistivity remains essentially unchanged despite variations in this spacing. This is a somewhat counterintuitive result, since naive expectations based on simple Coulomb interaction models would predict a strong dependence of drag strength on the distance separating the two layers, given that the Coulomb interaction strength decays with increasing separation. The theoretical work reveals that the inclusion of Fermi-liquid corrections effectively suppresses this expected spacing dependence, providing a mechanism that reconciles theory with the seemingly anomalous experimental observation of weak spacing dependence in real devices.

## Comparison with Experimental Observations

The theoretical predictions developed in this study are shown to align well with existing experimental data on Coulomb drag measurements taken in the vicinity of half-filling of the lowest Landau level. This agreement is significant because it validates the theoretical framework incorporating Fermi-liquid quasiparticle interactions as an essential ingredient for correctly describing drag physics in the composite fermion regime. The correspondence between theory and experiment, particularly regarding the temperature dependence, magnetic field dependence, and the notable insensitivity to interlayer spacing, lends strong support to the picture of composite fermions as interacting quasiparticles whose collective behavior governs the transresistivity in this strongly correlated quantum Hall system. This work thus contributes to a deeper understanding of many-body effects in composite fermion liquids and offers a theoretical foundation for interpreting drag experiments in double-layer quantum Hall systems near even-denominator filling fractions.

# Coulomb Drag Transresistivity Near Half-Filling of the Lowest Landau Level: The Role of Fermi-Liquid Interactions

## Introduction

Coulomb drag experiments in double-layer two-dimensional electron systems provide a sensitive probe of electron-electron interactions between spatially separated but Coulomb-coupled layers. In these measurements, a current is driven through one layer (the "active" layer), while the second, electrically isolated layer (the "passive" layer) develops a voltage due to momentum transfer mediated by interlayer Coulomb interactions. The resulting transresistivity is a direct measure of the strength and nature of interlayer correlations, and it has served as a valuable diagnostic tool for many-body phenomena in these systems, including the formation of composite fermions, the emergence of exciton condensates, and various other correlated electronic states.

Of particular interest is the behavior of Coulomb drag in the vicinity of half-filling of the lowest Landau level (ν = 1/2), where each layer, when considered in isolation, is believed to be well described by a composite fermion (CF) liquid. In this picture, electrons bind to two flux quanta of the applied magnetic field to form composite fermions that experience a strongly reduced effective magnetic field, leading to a Fermi-liquid-like state with well-defined quasiparticles despite the presence of a large external magnetic field. This composite fermion Fermi liquid has been the subject of extensive theoretical and experimental study, and Coulomb drag between two such half-filled layers offers a unique window into the interactions between composite fermions across the two layers.

Previous theoretical treatments of drag in the CF regime have typically employed a simplified model in which the quasiparticles are treated as effectively free fermions coupled only through the interlayer Coulomb interaction (screened by gauge-field fluctuations arising from the Chern-Simons transformation used to attach flux to the electrons). While this approach captures several qualitative features observed in experiments—such as the characteristic temperature and magnetic-field dependence of the transresistivity near ν = 1/2—it neglects an important ingredient: the residual Fermi-liquid interactions between quasiparticles within each layer. These interactions, encoded in Landau parameters, can substantially renormalize the quasiparticle properties (effective mass, compressibility, spin susceptibility) and are expected, on general grounds, to modify the drag response as well.

## Theoretical Framework

In this work, we develop a theoretical description of Coulomb drag between two closely spaced two-dimensional electron layers, each tuned near ν = 1/2, that explicitly incorporates Fermi-liquid interactions among the composite-fermion quasiparticles. Our starting point is the standard composite fermion framework, in which the physical electrons in each layer are mapped onto composite fermions via a singular gauge (Chern-Simons) transformation that attaches two flux quanta to each electron. At exactly ν = 1/2, the average effective magnetic field seen by the composite fermions vanishes, and the low-energy physics is that of a fermion system coupled to a fluctuating Chern-Simons gauge field, supplemented by the residual short-range Fermi-liquid interactions between the fermions.

The interlayer drag transresistivity is computed within the standard diagrammatic framework in which the leading Coulomb drag signal arises from the exchange of dynamically screened interlayer interactions between the two composite-fermion liquids. The key input to this calculation is the polarization function (density-density response function) of the composite-fermion liquid in each layer, dressed by both the gauge-field-mediated interactions and the Fermi-liquid interactions. We compute these interlayer and intralayer response functions within a self-consistent random-phase-type approximation, extended to include vertex corrections associated with the Fermi-liquid interactions, following the general formalism developed for single-layer composite fermion transport.

A central technical point of our analysis concerns how the Fermi-liquid interactions modify the effective interlayer coupling that enters the drag calculation. In the absence of these interactions, the transresistivity depends sensitively on the interlayer separation d, since the strength of the effective interlayer interaction (mediated by both direct Coulomb coupling and gauge-field fluctuations) is exponentially sensitive to d on the scale of the inter-particle spacing or the magnetic length. However, once Fermi-liquid corrections are properly included, we find that this sensitivity is substantially altered, primarily as a consequence of how these interactions renormalize the compressibility and effective mass entering the intralayer polarization functions, which in turn control the screening of the interlayer interaction.

## Key Results

We calculate the temperature (T) and magnetic-field (B) dependence of the transresistivity ρ_D over the range of parameters typically explored in experiments on double-layer GaAs-based two-dimensional electron systems near ν = 1/2. Our central results are as follows.

**Independence from interlayer spacing.** We find that, once Fermi-liquid interactions are included self-consistently in the composite fermion polarization functions, the calculated transresistivity becomes essentially independent of the interlayer spacing d, for values of d comparable to those used in typical drag experiments (of order the magnetic length or several times the effective Bohr radius). This is a striking result, since naive expectations based on the strength of the interlayer Coulomb (or gauge-field-mediated) interaction would suggest a strong, exponential-like dependence of ρ_D on d, as is indeed found in earlier theories that neglect Fermi-liquid corrections. We trace this cancellation to a compensating effect between the direct d-dependence of the interlayer coupling and the d-independent renormalization of the intralayer response functions by the Fermi-liquid interactions, which act to suppress or enhance the overall drag signal in a manner that largely offsets the explicit d-dependence of the bare interlayer interaction.

**Temperature and magnetic field scaling.** We find that the transresistivity exhibits a characteristic power-law-like temperature dependence at fixed magnetic field near ν = 1/2, consistent with the composite fermion Fermi liquid picture, but with a modified prefactor and exponent arising from the Fermi-liquid corrections to the quasiparticle self-energy and effective mass. As the magnetic field is tuned away from exact half-filling, the transresistivity is found to increase, reflecting the influence of the small non-zero effective field on the composite fermions and the associated modification of their scattering rate; we obtain the detailed dependence of this increase on the deviation from ν = 1/2 within our theoretical framework.

**Comparison with experiment.** We compare our theoretical predictions directly with existing experimental measurements of Coulomb drag in double-layer two-dimensional electron systems near ν = 1/2, spanning a range of interlayer separations, layer densities, and temperatures. We find good quantitative agreement between our calculated transresistivity and the measured values, both in terms of the overall magnitude of ρ_D and its temperature and magnetic-field dependence. Notably, our theory naturally accounts for the experimentally observed weak dependence of the transresistivity on interlayer spacing, a feature that is difficult to reconcile with earlier theoretical treatments that omit Fermi-liquid effects and that consequently predict a much stronger d-dependence than is observed.

## Discussion

These results underscore the importance of treating the full Fermi-liquid structure of the composite fermion liquid when computing transport and drag properties near even-denominator filling factors. While the basic composite fermion picture correctly captures the qualitative Fermi-liquid-like behavior of the ν = 1/2 state, quantitative comparison with drag experiments requires going beyond a free-fermion treatment of the quasiparticles to include the residual short-range interactions encoded in the Landau parameters. Our finding that these interactions render the transresistivity insensitive to interlayer spacing, in a manner consistent with experimental observations, provides strong support for the validity of the composite fermion Fermi-liquid description of the ν = 1/2 state, and highlights Coulomb drag as a particularly sensitive probe of Fermi-liquid interactions in these exotic quantum Hall systems.

More broadly, our work suggests that Fermi-liquid interaction effects, which are often treated as subleading corrections in single-layer transport phenomena, can play a qualitatively decisive role in interlayer transport phenomena such as Coulomb drag, where they control the delicate balance between direct interlayer coupling and intralayer screening. This observation may have implications for the interpretation of drag experiments in other correlated double-layer systems, including bilayer graphene and other Van der Waals heterostructures exhibiting composite-fermion physics, where similar Fermi-liquid corrections are expected to be important. Future experiments that systematically vary interlayer spacing over a wider range, or that probe the drag response away from exact half-filling with finer resolution, could provide further stringent tests of the theoretical framework developed here.

# The Coulomb-Hall Connection

Here we explore the fascinating relationship between Coulomb's law and the Hall effect, two fundamental phenomena in electromagnetism that reveal the intricate behavior of charged particles.

Coulomb's law, formulated by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785, describes the electrostatic force between charged particles. The law states that the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This elegant relationship forms the foundation for understanding electric fields and remains one of the cornerstones of classical electromagnetism.

The Hall effect, discovered by Edwin Hall in 1879, emerges when a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the current flow in a conductor, generating a voltage difference across the conductor. This phenomenon occurs due to the Lorentz force acting on the charge carriers, causing them to accumulate on one side of the material and creating a measurable Hall voltage.

While these two principles originate from different aspects of electromagnetic theory, they share a common thread: both fundamentally depend on the behavior of charged particles under the influence of electric and magnetic fields. Coulomb's law governs the static interactions between charges, establishing how they attract or repel one another based on their magnitudes and separation distance. The Hall effect, on the other hand, demonstrates how moving charges respond to magnetic fields, providing crucial insights into charge carrier density, sign, and mobility in materials.

Here, the interplay between these principles becomes particularly significant in semiconductor physics and materials science. Understanding Coulomb interactions helps explain the underlying charge distribution and electric fields within a material, while Hall effect measurements offer practical means to characterize these materials experimentally. Together, they provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing electronic properties, from simple conductors to complex semiconductor devices used in modern technology.

The synergy between Coulomb's foundational electrostatic principles and Hall's discovery of transverse voltage generation continues to influence contemporary research, particularly in areas like quantum Hall effects, spintronics, and the development of novel electronic materials with tailored electrical properties.

The magnetic field dependence of the transresistivity exhibits a sharp peak precisely at ν = 1/2, flanked by rapid suppression as the filling factor is tuned away from half-filling into the regime of well-formed fractional quantum Hall states, reflecting the destruction of the CF Fermi surface and the opening of an energy gap. We interpret these results within the framework of Chern-Simons composite fermion theory, in which drag arises from the exchange of transverse gauge bosons between the two layers, with the interlayer separation and layer density serving as key control parameters governing the crossover between gauge-field-mediated and Coulomb-mediated drag mechanisms. Our findings provide direct transport evidence for the applicability of the CF description at ν = 1/2 and establish Coulomb drag as a sensitive probe of the underlying quasiparticle dynamics and interlayer correlations in strongly correlated quantum Hall bilayers.

# Abstract

We present a theoretical analysis of Coulomb drag between two closely spaced two-dimensional electron systems at half-filled Landau levels, where each layer hosts a composite fermion (CF) Fermi sea. While the conventional composite fermion picture treats these quasiparticles as weakly interacting, we demonstrate that residual Fermi-liquid interactions among composite fermions play a decisive role in determining the transresistivity ρ₂₁ measured in drag experiments. Incorporating quasiparticle interaction corrections—analogous to Landau parameters in conventional Fermi liquids—into the CF transport theory, we find that these interactions renormalize the effective mass, compressibility, and current vertex of the composite fermions, leading to modifications of the drag transresistivity that persist even in the limit of large interlayer separation d relative to the magnetic length ℓ_B.

This behavior contrasts sharply with drag between ordinary (non-composite) Fermi liquids, where transresistivity arising from interlayer Coulomb scattering decays rapidly, typically as a high power of 1/d, once d exceeds the intralayer Fermi wavelength or screening length. We show that the gauge-field-mediated interactions intrinsic to the CF construction, combined with Fermi-liquid corrections to the quasiparticle scattering amplitude, generate a long-range contribution to the interlayer drag response that remains largely insensitive to d over the experimentally accessible range. We derive an analytic expression for ρ₂₁(T, B, d) within a diagrammatic CF transport formalism, incorporating both the singular gauge-field propagator and static Fermi-liquid corrections to the effective interaction, and show that the resulting temperature and magnetic-field dependence closely reproduces the anomalous drag signal observed at ν = 1/2 in bilayer heterostructures.

Our results provide a unified explanation for two previously puzzling experimental observations: (i) the anomalously large magnitude of drag at half-filling compared to the Fermi-liquid prediction, and (ii) its weak dependence on interlayer spacing over a wide range of d/ℓ_B. We conclude that Fermi-liquid corrections to the composite fermion quasiparticle interactions are not a small perturbation but rather an essential ingredient in quantitatively accounting for Coulomb drag phenomenology at even-denominator filling factors, and we discuss implications for the broader theory of interacting composite fermion liquids and their transport anomalies.

# Coulomb Drag in the Quantum Hall Regime: Fermi-Liquid Quasiparticle Interactions and Experimental Comparison

## Abstract

We investigate Coulomb drag between spatially separated two-dimensional electron systems in the quantum Hall regime, focusing on the role of Fermi-liquid quasiparticle renormalization in determining the magnitude and temperature dependence of the drag resistivity. Within a Fermi-liquid framework, we treat the interlayer Coulomb interaction perturbatively while incorporating quasiparticle lifetime effects, screening, and Landau-level mixing near integer and fractional filling factors. Our theory predicts characteristic oscillations in drag resistivity as a function of magnetic field, tracking the density of states at the Fermi level, with peak amplitudes exhibiting a distinct temperature scaling ($\rho_D \propto T^2$ in the Fermi-liquid regime, crossing over to non-monotonic behavior near half-filling of the lowest Landau level). We show that quasiparticle interaction corrections beyond the random-phase approximation are essential to reproduce the observed enhancement of drag near even-denominator filling fractions, where composite fermion quasiparticles dominate transport. Comparison with existing experimental drag measurements in GaAs/AlGaAs double-quantum-well heterostructures demonstrates quantitative agreement in the weak-coupling regime, while systematic deviations at strong magnetic fields point to the breakdown of simple Fermi-liquid quasiparticle pictures and the emergence of correlated composite-fermion drag mechanisms. These results clarify the interplay between single-particle and collective excitations in mediating interlayer momentum transfer and provide a benchmark for future theories of drag in strongly correlated quantum Hall systems.

---

# Abstract

We present a theoretical study of the temperature and magnetic field dependence of Coulomb drag (transresistivity) between two closely spaced two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) layers in the vicinity of Landau level filling factor ν = 1/2. Within the composite fermion (CF) picture, the drag resistivity ρ₂₁ arises from momentum transfer mediated by density and current fluctuations of composite fermions coupled to a fluctuating Chern-Simons gauge field. We calculate the transresistivity using a diagrammatic approach that incorporates the CF effective mass, gauge-field-mediated interactions, and screening effects, extending the zero-field Coulomb drag formalism to the composite fermion Fermi-liquid framework appropriate near ν = 1/2.

Our results show that ρ₂₁ scales approximately as T² at low temperatures, consistent with a Fermi-liquid-like quasiparticle picture, but with an enhanced prefactor relative to the B = 0 case due to the additional gauge-field-mediated interaction channel. As the magnetic field is tuned away from exact half-filling, we find a systematic evolution of the drag signal reflecting the interplay between the residual effective field acting on composite fermions and the interlayer separation, layer density, and temperature. We further examine the dependence of ρ₂₁ on interlayer distance d and demonstrate that the characteristic 1/d⁴ scaling expected from long-wavelength density fluctuations is modified by gauge-field contributions important at short distances.

The calculated magnitude and temperature dependence of the transresistivity are found to be in good quantitative agreement with experimental measurements on GaAs/AlGaAs double-quantum-well systems near ν = 1/2, supporting the validity of the composite fermion Fermi-liquid description of the half-filled Landau level and establishing Coulomb drag as a sensitive probe of gauge-field-mediated interactions between composite fermions in spatially separated layers.
